content: A nocturnal emission refers to the involuntary ejaculation of semen that occurs during sleep in males. This phenomenon is also commonly known as a wet dream or an orgasm during sleep. It is most frequently observed during adolescence and early adulthood, although it can occur at any point after puberty. Nocturnal emissions may or may not be accompanied by erotic dreams, and the ejaculation can occur even in the absence of an erection. Some individuals may wake up during the event, while others may remain asleep throughout the process. In some cases, these episodes are referred to as sex dreams. It is important to note that women can also experience orgasms during sleep. The frequency of nocturnal emissions varies significantly among individuals. Some males report experiencing numerous nocturnal emissions during their teenage years, while others may never experience one. In the United States, approximately 83% of men will experience a nocturnal emission at some point in their lives. In cultures where masturbation is less socially accepted, such as in certain non-Western countries, surveys indicate that up to 98% of men eventually experience nocturnal emissions. Among males who do experience them, the average frequency ranges from 0.36 times per week for single 15-year-olds to 0.18 times per week for single 40-year-olds. For married males, the average frequency is slightly lower, ranging from 0.23 times per week for 19-year-olds to 0.15 times per week for 50-year-olds. Some individuals experience nocturnal emissions only during a specific period of their lives, while others may continue to have them throughout adulthood. There is no definitive link between the frequency of nocturnal emissions and the frequency of masturbation. Alfred Kinsey, a prominent sex researcher, observed that males with higher rates of nocturnal emissions often reported lower rates of masturbation. Some individuals attribute their frequent nocturnal emissions to abstaining from masturbation, but it is equally plausible that the reverse is true—that they masturbate less because they experience frequent emissions. For women, the relationship between nocturnal orgasms and sexual activity is similarly inconclusive. Kinsey's research found that women who experienced a sudden reduction in the frequency of coital orgasms only had a slight increase in the number of orgasms during sleep. Testosterone levels can influence the frequency of nocturnal emissions. A 1998 study demonstrated that the number of boys reporting nocturnal emissions increased significantly with higher doses of testosterone. For example, 17% of participants reported nocturnal emissions without testosterone treatment, compared to 90% at high doses. During puberty, approximately 13% of males experience their first ejaculation as a result of a nocturnal emission. Kinsey's research also found that males who experienced their first ejaculation through a nocturnal emission were generally older than those who first ejaculated through masturbation. This suggests that the onset of ejaculation via nocturnal emission may be delayed by a year or more compared to what is developmentally possible through physical stimulation. Unlike typical ejaculations, which often terminate an erection, nocturnal emissions may leave the individual with a functional erection afterward. Although various treatments and remedies have been proposed to prevent or reduce nocturnal emissions, none have undergone rigorous scientific testing or received regulatory approval, such as from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). These remedies are often comparable to unproven home cures for conditions like hiccups. Since nocturnal emissions do not cause physical harm beyond the inconvenience of cleaning up and are not indicative of any underlying medical condition, treatment is generally considered unnecessary. Involuntary orgasms can also occur during waking hours in both sexes, but such events are rare. Regarding women, a 1953 study by Kinsey found that 40% of women had experienced at least one orgasm during sleep by the age of 45. A 1986 study published in the Journal of Sex Research reported that 85% of women who experienced sleep orgasms first did so at a young age, often before the age of 21, and in some cases before the age of 13. Historically, frequent involuntary orgasms or excessive semen discharge in males were diagnosed as a condition called spermatorrhoea or seminal weakness during the 18th and 19th centuries. Treatments for this so-called disease included medications, circumcision, and even castration. While some modern practitioners, particularly herbalists, continue to diagnose and treat cases of spermatorrhoea, these treatments lack scientific validation and are not supported by rigorous research. Religious perspectives on nocturnal emissions have varied. Saint Augustine, for example, argued that nocturnal emissions, unlike masturbation, did not corrupt a man's conscience because they were involuntary and not deliberate acts of lust. However, he prayed for divine assistance to overcome what he described as the glue of lust. In the Bible, nocturnal emissions are indirectly referenced using the Hebrew term tameh, often translated as impure. According to Levitical law, individuals who experienced a nocturnal emission were required to bathe in a mikveh (ritual bath) and were considered ceremonially unclean until sunset. Similar rules applied to men who had sexual intercourse with their wives, as well as to women during menstruation or after childbirth. On Yom Kippur, a day when bathing is prohibited, psalms are traditionally recited at night as a supposed safeguard against nocturnal emissions. However, some biblical references to emissions may pertain to discharges of blood or other substances indicative of disease, rather than semen. The Bible distinguishes between normal emissions, which require purification until nightfall, and abnormal discharges, which necessitate a week-long purification process. In medieval Western occultism, nocturnal emissions were sometimes attributed to encounters with succubi—mythical female demons believed to engage in sexual activity with individuals during sleep. These events were often associated with night terrors and other supernatural explanations.
